extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, and evidentiary criteria governing disciplinary proceedings before the USPTO (OED Director v. practitioner), including statute of limitations, discovery, burdens of proof, sanctions, and aggravating/mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations start date for USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO disciplinary proceedings must be commenced no later than 1 year after the date on which the misconduct forming the basis for the proceeding is made known to an officer or employee of the Office. The limitations period begins when the OED Director receives a 'grievance.' (35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treats the date the OED Director receives a written grievance (as defined by regulation) as the triggering event. Tolling agreements can extend the deadline (example: parties agreed to extend from July 23, 2020 to January 4, 2021). Knowledge of related discipline in another jurisdiction alone does not necessarily start the clock for misconduct occurring elsewhere; OED must have received a grievance presenting possible grounds for discipline of the specified practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'grievance' under 37 C.F.R. § 11.1
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'grievance' is defined as 'a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only receipt of such a written submission by the OED Director triggers the regulatory statute-of-limitations condition; discovery or other investigative materials before OED's receipt do not automatically count as starting the limitations period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the violation by clear and convincing evidence; the respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is an intermediate standard—more than preponderance but less than beyond a reasonable doubt—requiring evidence that produces a 'firm belief or conviction' that the facts are 'highly probable' (citing Jimenez; Colorado v. New Mexico).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard (Rule 56 applied via 37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is appropriate where the movant shows there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and is entitled to judgment as a matter of law (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a), as applied by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must view evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. An issue is 'genuine' only if a reasonable factfinder could return a verdict for either party; a fact is 'material' only if it could affect the outcome under governing law. Summary judgment is inappropriate where material facts are susceptible to divergent inferences; but may be appropriate where a party with the burden fails to make a sufficient showing on an essential element (Celotex; Anderson; Tolan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal for fraud or abuse of process is an extreme sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: A court has inherent power to dismiss an action when a party deceives the court or abuses the process at a level that undermines the integrity of the process, but dismissal is the most extreme sanction and must be entered 'with the greatest caution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before dismissing for fraud/abuse, courts should consider availability of lesser sanctions and multiple factors (citing Projects Mgmt. v. Dyncorp Int’l LLC; Shaffer Equip.). Dismissal requires clear evidence of deception or abuse sufficient to render dismissal proportionate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery authorization and scope under 37 C.F.R. § 11.52
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in USPTO disciplinary proceedings is authorized under 37 C.F.R. § 11.52, subject to the Court's control and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery requests must be narrowly tailored and tied to specific material issues raised in the pleadings. Overbroad requests that seek 'all documents related to any' matter (example: proposed RFP 4(i)) are subject to denial as not sufficiently specific or relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer requirement and compliance with court orders (37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must confer with opposing counsel before filing motions as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.43, and must obey court orders restricting filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with the meet-and-confer requirement or express court orders may result in summary denial of motions; the Court may nevertheless exercise discretion and warn parties before imposing the harsh remedy of summary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of hearsay in USPTO administrative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearsay evidence is admissible in this administrative disciplinary proceeding and the Confrontation Clause does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence such as declarations signed under penalty of perjury may be admissible even if the witness cannot be located; the inability to confront a witness does not automatically require striking claims in an administrative context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards to identify aggravating and mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal often looks to the ABA's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when determining whether aggravating or mitigating factors exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate the record and parties' arguments against the ABA Standards framework to decide which factors are present and to weigh them in determining an appropriate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: prior disciplinary history (ABA Standards § 9.22(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior disciplinary history is an aggravating factor when determining sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior offenses that relate to the instant misconduct may lessen the impact somewhat, but prior discipline generally increases the severity of sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: dishonest or selfish motive (ABA Standards § 9.22(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonest or selfish motive is an aggravating factor supporting more severe sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct motivated by pecuniary gain or intentional exploitation (e.g., ignoring warnings to profit) weighs toward harsher discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: pattern of misconduct and multiple offenses (ABA Standards § 9.22(c), (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of misconduct and multiple offenses are aggravating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failures (e.g., prolonged failure to supervise non-lawyer staff resulting in numerous rule violations) support heightened sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: bad faith obstruction and refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing (ABA Standards § 9.22(e), (g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad faith obstruction of disciplinary proceedings and refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of conduct are aggravating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dragging feet, ignoring or failing to obey orders, and generally obstructive conduct during the process increase sanction severity; a later partial acknowledgment may temper but not eliminate this aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: vulnerability of victims (ABA Standards § 9.22(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting or harming vulnerable victims is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploiting populations at special risk (e.g., low-wage immigrant workers fearing deportation) weighs heavily toward more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factor: relative inexperience (ABA Standards § 9.32(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative inexperience in the practice of law can be a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A respondent's early-career status and resulting vulnerability to deception or poor judgment may reduce the level of discipline imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors: delay in proceedings and imposition of other penalties (ABA Standards § 9.32(j), (k))
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in the disciplinary proceeding and the fact that other penalties or sanctions have been imposed elsewhere can be mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protracted timeline and prior penalties (e.g., civil restitution, state bar actions) may be taken into account to lessen the ultimate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factor: remorse (ABA Standards § 9.32(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression of remorse for harming innocent people is a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remorse must be meaningful and accompanied by concrete regard for victims to be a substantial mitigation; perfunctory or limited remorse has less weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to confirm identity before initiating action based on discipline databases
rubrics_metrics.description: When an OED analyst retrieves names from external disciplinary databanks, OED should confirm identity before acting because the databank entry may relate to a different person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirming identity (e.g., verifying that the disciplined attorney in another jurisdiction is the same USPTO practitioner) is reasonable and necessary; OED's confirmation within a short period (less than a month in the example) supports a finding that action was timely and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege log and Privacy Act redactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Redactions made to avoid violating the Privacy Act (5 U.S.C. § 552a) are permissible and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure are not binding in this administrative forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A privilege log explaining redactions to protect privacy is acceptable; redacted material may also be irrelevant to the proceeding, and challenges to the log must explain specific prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for reconsideration of discovery rulings (narrow tailoring and materiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests to reconsider discovery denials must show the original ruling was erroneous; discovery must be narrowly tailored and tied to specific material issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overbroad discovery demands (e.g., 'all documents related to any immigration matter of' victims) that are not tied to material issues will be denied and are not grounds for reconsideration without a showing of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate sanctioning requires proportionality and consideration of comparators
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should be proportionate to the misconduct, informed by aggravating and mitigating factors, and may be guided by comparisons to similar cases (e.g., range from admonition to exclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal may distinguish comparable cases (e.g., another attorney receiving only admonition where facts differ) and choose an intermediate sanction (example: 18-month suspension rather than exclusion) when mitigators and aggravators are balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights and finality under USPTO regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may appeal the initial decision to the USPTO Director by filing a notice of appeal within 14 days; absent appeal, the decision becomes final per 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(d) and related provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely filing is required to invoke appellate review; regulatory provisions (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55(a), 11.54(d)) control appeal timing and finality.
